events.title: The march from Williamsburg
events.text: At five in the morning of 28 September the allied army, 8,000 Americans and 7,800 French, leaves Williamsburg. The Continentals take the right fork for the Hampton road, the French the left. About noon the van meets British pickets two miles from the works; Tarleton's cavalry trades a few cannon shots on the Moore House side and pulls back at sunset.

events.title: The investment
events.text: By nightfall the army lies on its arms in a half-circle from the York above the town to Wormley Creek below it: Americans on the right, French on the left, Beaverdam Creek between them. Cornwallis holds an outer line on the high ground between the creeks and the inner works around the town. He has 8,000 men, 65 guns in the works, and Clinton's promise of a relief fleet.

events.title: Skirmishing
events.text: The American wing shifts right and camps east of Beaverdam Creek within cannon shot; riflemen trade fire with the Ansbach pickets at Pigeon Hill. That night Cornwallis, trusting Clinton's letter that help will sail about 5 October, abandons his outer works and pulls everything inside the town line except the Fusiliers' Redoubt and Redoubts 9 and 10.

events.title: The outer works taken
events.text: At first light the empty redoubts are found. Bourbonnais grenadiers and Deux-Ponts chasseurs occupy the Pigeon Quarter works, Lafayette's light infantry the field work on the Hampton road. Saint-Simon's volunteers drive in the pickets before the Fusiliers' Redoubt and are thrown back. Colonel Scammell, reconnoitring, is shot after surrendering and dies at Williamsburg.

events.title: Gabions and fascines
events.text: For six days a third of the army cuts stakes and weaves gabions and fascines, 6,000 stakes, 2,000 fascines and 600 gabions, while the siege train comes up by ox team from Trebell's Landing on the James. The British fire three hundred shot a day and kill a man or two. On 3 October at Gloucester, Lauzun's hussars unhorse Tarleton and shut the garrison inside its lines.

events.title: The first parallel
events.text: On a dark, wet night 1,500 men dig while 2,800 stand to arms. Washington strikes the first pickaxe. The Touraine regiment makes a false attack on the upper river that draws the British fire. By dawn a trench 2,000 yards long, 600 to 800 yards from the works, covers the diggers, and the enemy, Washington writes, were totally ignorant of our labour until daylight.

events.title: Batteries
events.text: Two days to finish the parallel, its four redoubts and the batteries, and to drag in the guns. The trenches are relieved every twenty-four hours, the Americans by division, the French by two regiments at a time.

events.title: The guns open
events.text: At three in the afternoon of 9 October the French battery on the far left opens on the Fusiliers' Redoubt and the ships. At five Washington puts the match to the first gun of the Grand American Battery on the right. By morning the British have pulled their pieces back from the embrasures.

events.title: Bombardment
events.text: The Grand French Battery and Machin's battery open at daylight: fifty-two allied guns and mortars by the 11th, firing round the clock. The British reply falls to six shots an hour. Cornwallis moves his headquarters from the Nelson house to a cave in the bluff. That night French hot shot sets the 44-gun Charon ablaze with two transports.

events.title: The second parallel
events.text: Steuben's division and the Gâtinais and Deux-Ponts regiments open the second parallel 300 yards from the works, 750 yards long by morning. It cannot reach the river: Redoubts 9 and 10 stand in the way and enfilade its right. For three days the guns batter their abatis.

events.title: The night of 14 October
events.text: Moonless. Four hundred French under Deux-Ponts form against Redoubt 9, four hundred Americans under Hamilton against Redoubt 10, muskets unloaded, bayonets fixed. Diversions are fired at the Fusiliers' Redoubt and at Gloucester. At eight o'clock six shells rise from the batteries: the signal.

events.title: Redoubts 9 and 10
events.text: Hamilton's men go through the abatis without waiting for the sappers and are over the parapet in ten minutes; Laurens's party comes round behind and takes Major Campbell. The French halt at the abatis under fire while the carpenters cut, then charge: seven minutes of fighting and the Hessians throw down their arms. Nine Americans and fifteen French are killed; the redoubts cost Cornwallis eighteen dead and seventy-three prisoners.

events.title: To the river
events.text: Overnight the parallel is dug through both redoubts to the bluff, and by evening howitzers in them fire into the town from 300 yards. Cornwallis writes to Clinton that the safety of the place is so precarious that he cannot recommend the fleet and army should run great risk to save him.

events.title: The sortie
events.text: Before dawn on the 16th Abercrombie leads 350 Guards, grenadiers and light infantry out of the Hornwork against the junction of the parallels. They spike four French guns and two American with bayonet points and are driven out by Noailles's grenadiers crying Vive le Roi. The spikes are drilled out and the guns are firing again by noon.

events.title: The boats
events.text: Cornwallis's last throw: sixteen boats to carry the fit men over to Gloucester, break through Choisy, and march for New York. The light infantry, most of the Guards and the 23rd cross before midnight. Then the weather changes from moderate and calm to a most violent storm of wind and rain and drives the second trip down the river.

events.title: The storm
events.text: At two in the morning the wind moderates. Cornwallis calls the troops back; the boats return after daybreak under fire from the batteries and the detachment is in the lines again by noon. A hundred allied pieces are now in action, the fraises are falling and breaches have begun.

events.title: The drummer
events.text: At ten o'clock on 17 October a drummer in red mounts the Hornwork parapet and beats a parley, and an officer comes out with a flag. Cornwallis asks for twenty-four hours and commissioners to meet at Mr Moore's house. Washington gives him two hours to put his proposals in writing. The guns stop in the afternoon.

events.title: The Moore House
events.text: Dundas and Ross for the British, Noailles and Laurens for the allies, sit all afternoon and into the night at the Moore House. The terms are those Cornwallis's army gave Lincoln at Charleston: the garrison marches out with colours cased and the band may not play an American or French march.

events.title: 19 October 1781
events.text: The articles are signed in the trenches at eleven. At noon two redoubts on the British left are handed over, one to Butler's Americans, one to Laval's French. The allied army forms along the Hampton road for over a mile, Americans on the east side, French on the west.

events.title: The world turned upside down
events.text: At two o'clock the garrison marches out under O'Hara, Cornwallis pleading illness, drums beating a British march. O'Hara offers his sword to Rochambeau, who points him to Washington, who points him to Lincoln. In the field at the end of the road 7,247 soldiers and 840 seamen ground their arms. At three the Gloucester garrison does the same before Choisy.

events.title: After
events.text: The prisoners march back into the town and set off for Winchester and Frederick two days later. The siege cost the British 156 killed and 326 wounded, the allies about 88 killed and 300 wounded. Clinton's fleet with 7,000 men sails from New York the same day and turns back at the Chesapeake. The war in America is, in effect, over.

losses: 156 killed, 326 wounded; 7,247 soldiers and 840 seamen surrendered.
outcome.note: The Gloucester garrison surrendered to Choisy the same afternoon.

sources: Earl Cornwallis to Sir Henry Clinton, York Town, 20 October 1781: the outer works, the sortie, the boats and the storm, the parley.
George Washington's diary, 28 September to 19 October 1781 (Founders Online): the first parallel, the hours the batteries opened, the storming of the redoubts, the howitzers of the 15th.
Journal of the Siege of York-town by the French General Staff (Gallatin), William and Mary 1931: the French trench rotation, battery by battery, with the daily French losses.
Guillaume de Deux-Ponts, My Campaigns in America (1868): the assault on Redoubt 9 in his own words, and Viomenil's report.
Banastre Tarleton, History of the Campaigns of 1780 and 1781 (1787), with Despard's return of 156 killed, 326 wounded and 70 missing.
Sebastian Bauman, Plan of the Investment of York and Gloucester (surveyed 22-28 October 1781, published 1782): the legend naming every battery and the day it opened.
Henry P. Johnston, The Yorktown Campaign and the Surrender of Cornwallis (1881): camps, regimental strengths, the sectors of the British line, the trench rotation.
Charles E. Hatch, Yorktown and the Siege of 1781 (NPS Historical Handbook 14, 1957); NPS Historic Resource Study Yorktown's Main Street (the British works lot by lot).
James Thacher, Military Journal; Ebenezer Denny, Military Journal; Stephan Popp's journal (Bayreuth regiment); Joseph Plumb Martin, A Narrative.

National Park Service, Yorktown Battlefield: the reconstructed British line, Redoubts 9 and 10, the Grand French Battery and the second parallel, as mapped in OpenStreetMap. Terrain: USGS 3DEP, 10 m, with the river at sea level.

What is reconstructed: the allied earthworks are 1930s rebuilds on sites fixed by archaeology; the visible British line is the 1862 Confederate rebuild over the 1781 one; Redoubts 1 to 8 are placed within about fifty metres; the French camp order by regiment is inferred from Ewald's plan; the trench guard is shown as one standing block for whichever division was on duty; the hours of the sortie (midnight to five) and the length of the fight for Redoubt 9 (seven minutes to half an hour) are given differently by every diarist.
